newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: World coffee markets see decade of rising demand.
newsitem.headline: World coffee markets see decade of rising demand.

text.p: Coffee drinkers are likely to face higher prices for a quality cup of their favourite beverage as industry experts predicted rising global demand for at least a decade.

Senior industry officials, traders and roasters at an international Tea and Coffee Symposium last week saw a bright future for the market, with high potential for growth in both the new markets of Asia and Eastern Europe as well as the more expensive high-quality gourmet coffee sector.
They warned that increased demand would mean consumers could expect to see higher average prices in future and wondered how the increased demand would be met.
Predictions at the meeting in Vienna by Brazil's largest co-operative pointed to growth not only in new markets but also in established coffee-drinking Western nations.

An increase of 1.4 percent per year is expected in traditional coffee-drinking countries whereas in emerging ones the forecast is 3.4 percent, the Cooperative Regional de Cafeicultores em Guaxupe Ltda (CRCG) said.
"An exception is made for China where a consumption increase of 12 percent per year is expected," said the co-operative, the largest in the world of coffee with 7,000 members.
"In emerging consuming countries, soluble coffee will be the major reason for the increase in consumption," it added.
Roasters, traders and officials also agreed an increased market share of global coffee consumption of some 100 million 60-kg bags would be taken by the gourmet market.
High-quality mild washed arabicas, the biggest source of coffee for the gourmet market, represent some 37 percent of global production.

Ted Lingle, executive director of the Specialty Coffee Association of America, said growing demand for high-quality coffee was certain to push up the average price for mild arabicas within the near future.

"Coffee in the 21st century is going to be very high quality and it's a trend which is growing at a much faster rate than our availability to grow it, so we are going to see much higher prices for good qualities.

"Consumer demand for good quality coffee will not go away, but where is the coffee going to come from? There is a real long-term supply problem for the high-quality coffee which will push prices," Lingle told Reuters.
He said recent wild fluctuations in coffee on the New York and London markets "signalled that we are going towards a much higher price level. The average price is going to be higher."

Joaquim Libanio Fereira Leite, export director of the Brazilian Co-operative CRCG, estimated an increase of 5-10 million 60-kg bags in world demand for mild washed arabicas over the next five to 10 years.

"There is a bright future for the high-quality coffee market. There is a demand for better quality coffee, even in Brazil among local consumers," he said. Brazil is the world's biggest coffee consumer in overall quantity.

"The number of people preferring a good cup of coffee is higher today than 10 years ago," said Italian coffee expert Alberto Hesse Trieste, predicting that the trend would continue beyond the year 2000.

While the industry expressed great hope for seeing high consumption growth in Asian countries, in particular China, German Coffee Association President and board member of Germany's top roaster Tchibo, Hasso Kaempfe, said Eastern Europe remained a key market.

"There is no law saying that coffee consumption will keep growing forever. There is however the possibility that new markets in Central and Eastern Europe will contribute to a growth of world wide coffee consumption which would be beneficial for everybody involved," he said.
